source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module C unit 4 (courseware unit 16): special cases of valuation

facts.statement: Intangible assets (courseware): intangible assets include goodwill, brand name, devoted employees and technological capability; accounting standards often understate or ignore them. Independent, cash-flow-generating intangibles are patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences and franchises: their value is the cash flows from the exclusive right over its finite life (typically no terminal value), found by discounted cash flow or by a multiple of the revenue or income from comparable assets; the costs of enforcing exclusivity and the chance of infringement reduce value. A franchise gives the right to sell a branded good under the franchisor name in return for an initial fee and an annual charge. Intangibles that do not generate cash flows on their own, such as brand name, can be valued by three approaches: capital investment (capitalising past spending such as advertising, the least subjective but possibly far from market value), discounted cash flow (the increase in cash flows attributable to the asset, discounted at a suitable rate) and relative valuation (comparing the market value of a company with the brand with that of similar companies without it).

Real estate firms (courseware): real estate and financial assets share the principle that value depends on the cash flows, their growth and their risk, so intrinsic and relative valuation apply; real estate has a finite life for buildings but the land has an endless life and may dominate terminal value. DCF valuation needs a discount rate and expected cash flows. The cost of equity can be found with CAPM or multifactor models; critics say real estate investors are not well diversified, but the courseware answers that investment concentration is a strategic choice, real estate can be subdivided into smaller parcels and securitised, and diversified institutions (real estate investment trusts, partnerships, corporations) are likely to become the marginal investors. Beta for real assets is hard to measure, because it needs a history of prices and returns against an index.

Start-up firms (courseware): valuation principles are unchanged: value is the present value of expected cash flows, but information is scarce. Information comes from the latest financial statements, the firm's history and its competitors or peers; start-ups have short histories, little disclosure and often no peers. Framework: (1) assess the current standing using the latest twelve months data in preference to the last financial year; (2) estimate revenue growth (high but decreasing as size grows, depending on market growth and barriers to entry or competitive advantage); (3) estimate the stable-growth operating margin from competitors and the income statement (start-up spending on growth is largely a capital expense); (4) estimate reinvestment: expected growth = reinvestment rate x return on capital, and where operating earnings are negative use the sales-to-capital ratio: expected reinvestment = expected change in revenue / (sales / capital), for example a ratio of 5 means Rs 2 lakh of capital for each Rs 10 lakh of extra revenue; in stable growth, reinvestment rate = stable growth / stable return on capital; (5) risk and discount rate: use bottom-up beta from comparable firms and a synthetic rating for the cost of debt, with beta moving towards 1 and the debt cost towards a mature firm as the firm grows; (6) value the firm, where the terminal value holds most of the value and depends on the growth and margin assumptions; account for survival: value of firm = probability of survival x DCF value + (1 - probability of survival) x distress or liquidation value; value non-operating assets (cash burn is fast); (7) deduct non-equity claims and value outstanding options with an option pricing model before dividing by the number of shares, allowing for dilution from future issues.

Firms with negative or low earnings (courseware): the way to value depends on why earnings are negative. Temporary problems (a strike, a product recall) or company-specific one-offs: remove the cost of the event and use normalised earnings, remembering tax effects. Industry-wide or cyclical problems: use normalised earnings, since the current year is deceptive. Long-term problems (obsolete plant, an untrained workforce, poor past investment): judge whether the problem can be solved and when; strategic blunders (the courseware cites Kodak, IBM and Xerox) may mean the firm never regains lost ground, so revenue growth and margins should be reduced; operating inefficiency is addressed by raising margins towards the industry average, and the speed depends on the firm size (a firm with revenue of Rs 1,000 crore needs to cut cost by Rs 50 crore for a 5 per cent margin gain while one with Rs 100 crore needs Rs 5 crore), the nature of the inefficiency (replacing machinery is quicker than retraining), external limits (union contracts, government) and the quality of management. For heavily indebted firms, the risk of default must be considered.

Financial service companies (courseware): banks earn the margin between interest paid and charged; insurers earn premiums and investment income; investment banks and wealth managers earn fees. Special features: debt is the raw material, so debt and reinvestment are hard to define; heavy regulation and capital adequacy norms; provisioning for losses affects income; difficulty choosing multiples; government directives on the financial mix. DCF models: use dividend discount, cash flow to equity or excess return models. Dividend model inputs: cost of equity (regression betas can be used if regulation is stable; bottom-up beta uses the average levered beta of comparable firms because financial firms are highly levered and debt is hard to measure); payout ratio (dividends over earnings; financial firms pay higher payout because regulatory capital needs mean lower net capital expenditure and investors prefer reliable payers; include buybacks by taking a composite payout over several years because buybacks vary); expected growth (historical earnings growth, analyst estimates, or fundamental growth = retention ratio x return on equity, and with a changing ROE: retention x ROE(t+1) + (ROE(t+1) - ROE(t)) / ROE(t)); in stable growth the payout ratio = 1 - g / ROE(stable) and beta should move towards 1. Asset-based valuation: value the loan portfolio (for example as the present value of the coupons at the fair market rate plus the present value of the principal) and deduct deposits, debt and other claims; it is hard when the firm operates across many businesses.

Distressed firms (courseware): where earnings are negative and debt is large, equity holders have limited liability and the option to liquidate, so equity is like a call option on the firm: payoff to equity on liquidation = V - D if V is greater than D, and 0 if V is at most D, where V is the value of the firm and D the face value of debt and other non-equity claims. The exercise price is the face value of debt and the option expires when the debt matures. Implications: equity can have value even when the firm value is below the debt (time value, as with an out-of-the-money option), and, unlike in DCF, higher risk can raise equity value because equity holders have little to lose and much to gain from variability.

Cash and cross holdings (courseware): non-operating assets include cash and near-cash (short-term government securities, commercial paper), investments in other companies and idle land or surplus pension assets; they receive little attention but have value. Reasons for holding cash (Keynes): transactions, precaution and speculation; the transaction need is higher for cash-oriented businesses (restaurants, groceries) than credit-oriented ones, lower for large-transaction businesses, and reduces as digital payment grows; managers may also hoard cash. Valuation approaches: consolidated (value the firm as a whole with cash inside: earnings include interest on cash, reinvestment covers cash, the unlevered beta is the weighted average of operating assets and cash, and the final valuation already includes cash, so do not add it) versus separate (value the operating assets alone: exclude interest income from cash, reinvest only in operating assets, use the beta of operating assets only, and add cash to the value of operating assets).

Warrants and convertibles (courseware): convertible bonds and preferred stock contain a call option letting the holder convert into common equity at a set price; because their value depends on the equity value, they cannot simply be subtracted from enterprise value as debt; the assumption that all target convertibles convert is reasonable when the offer price exceeds the conversion price. Their valuation has been dealt with in an earlier chapter (option pricing).

Cyclical firms and holding companies (courseware): earnings of cyclical companies depend heavily on the base year. Remedies: adjust expected growth (for example higher growth in the near term if earnings are depressed and recovery is expected; this depends on predicting the economy, with turning-point years estimated from past recessions) or normalise earnings (what would the company earn in a typical year). Methods of normalising: average the company's earnings over a full cycle (typically five to ten years), best for companies whose size has not changed; average the return on investment or margins over past periods and apply them to current capital or revenue (which adjusts for current size, with revenue-based margins less open to accounting manipulation); and, if it takes several periods for earnings to recover, reduce the value for the periods needed. Holding companies can be valued with free cash flow and dividend discount models and for their investment and strategic ability; e-commerce firms are valued by considering future technology, buyers' habits, the advantages and disadvantages of e-commerce and competitors. The courseware cautions that special categories (real estate, start-ups, negative earnings, cyclical, distressed, holding and e-commerce firms) need careful, specialised valuation.

payload.title: Intangible assets and how to value them
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Intangibles** (goodwill, brand, skilled people, technology) are often **understated or ignored** in accounts.

**Cash-flow-generating intangibles** (patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences, **franchises**): value the **cash flows from the exclusive right over its finite life**, usually with **no terminal value**, by **DCF** or a **multiple** from comparable assets. Reduce value for **enforcement costs** and **infringement**.

**Brand name and similar:** **capital investment** (capitalise past spend, such as advertising; **least subjective** but far from market value), **DCF** (the **extra cash flow** attributable to the asset) or **relative** (compare firms **with and without** the brand).

payload.title: Valuing real estate firms
payload.core_explanation_md:
Real and financial assets share the principle that **value depends on cash flows, growth and risk**, so **intrinsic and relative valuation** apply.

**Differences:** **buildings have a finite life**, but **land lasts for ever** and can dominate the **terminal value**.

**Cost of equity:** use **CAPM or multifactor models**. Critics say property investors are **not diversified**; the courseware replies that concentration is a **choice**, property can be **subdivided and securitised**, and **diversified institutions** (REITs, partnerships) are likely to be the **marginal investors**. **Beta** for real assets is hard to measure for lack of a **price history** against an index.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The value of the land component may matter more than the building in the final value.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can land dominate the terminal value of a real estate firm?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because land has an endless life while buildings wear out.

payload.title: Valuing a start-up: reinvestment and survival
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Information is thin**, so use the **latest twelve months**, peer margins and bottom-up betas.

**Reinvestment when earnings are negative:** **expected reinvestment = expected change in revenue / (sales-to-capital ratio)**. A ratio of **5** means **Rs 2 lakh of capital for each Rs 10 lakh of extra revenue**.

**Growth** (when earnings are positive): **expected growth = reinvestment rate x return on capital**; in **stable growth**: **reinvestment rate = stable growth / stable ROC**.

**Survival:** **value of firm = P(survive) x DCF value + (1 - P(survive)) x distress or liquidation value.**

**Terminal value** holds most of the value, so the **growth and margin assumptions** matter most.

payload.title: Asset-based valuation of a financial institution
payload.core_explanation_md:
Value the **loan portfolio** at **fair market value**: the **present value of its coupons at the market rate plus the present value of the principal**. Then **deduct deposits, debt and other claims** to get the **equity**.

A loan book earning **more than the market rate** is worth **more than book value**.

**Drawbacks:** it ignores **future growth and excess returns**, and it is **hard for firms in many businesses** (insurance, banking, investment banking) at once.

payload.title: Equity as a call option in distressed firms
payload.core_explanation_md:
For a **distressed** firm with large debt, equity holders have **limited liability** and the option to **liquidate**.

**Payoff to equity = V - D if V > D; 0 if V is at most D**, where **V** is the firm value and **D** the **face value of debt and other claims**. The **exercise price** is the **debt's face value**; the option **expires when the debt matures**.

**Implications:** equity can have value **even when V is below D** (time value), and **higher risk can raise equity value**, unlike in DCF.

payload.title: Cash, cross holdings and consolidated versus separate valuation
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Non-operating assets:** **cash and near-cash**, **stakes in other firms**, **idle land**, **surplus pension assets**.

**Why hold cash (Keynes):** **transactions**, **precaution**, **speculation**; also **managers may hoard**. Cash needs are **higher for cash businesses** (restaurants), **lower for firms with large transactions** and fall with **digital payments**.

**Consolidated valuation:** cash is treated as **inside** the firm: earnings include **interest on cash**; beta is a **weighted average** for the operating assets and the cash; so cash is **not added a second time**.

**Separate valuation:** **operating assets only**; **exclude interest on cash**; **add cash** to the value of operations.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Both routes should give the same value if applied consistently.

self_check.prompt_text: Under separate valuation, what is done with cash?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is excluded from operations and added to the value of the operating assets.

payload.title: Warrants and convertibles
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **convertible bond or preferred share** carries a **call option** to convert into equity at a **fixed price**.

Because its value **depends on the equity value**, it **cannot simply be deducted as debt** from enterprise value. If an **offer price exceeds the conversion price**, treating all convertibles as **converted** is reasonable.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Their value is found with option pricing methods.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a convertible not be treated purely as debt?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Its value depends on the company equity value through the conversion option.

payload.title: Cyclical firms: normalising earnings
payload.core_explanation_md:
Earnings in the **base year** can mislead for cyclical firms. **Remedies:** **adjust expected growth** (for example **higher near-term growth** when earnings are depressed), or **normalise earnings**: **what would the firm earn in a typical year?**

**Methods:** **average earnings over a full cycle** (**five to ten years**); **average the ROC or margin** over past periods and **apply it to current capital or revenue**, which adjusts for **current size** (revenue-based margins are **harder to manipulate**); and if recovery takes **several periods**, **reduce value for the delay**.

**Normalised earnings = average return on capital x current capital.**

items.title: Intangible assets and how to value them
items.core_explanation_md:
**Intangibles** (goodwill, brand, skilled people, technology) are often **understated or ignored** in accounts.

**Cash-flow-generating intangibles** (patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences, **franchises**): value the **cash flows from the exclusive right over its finite life**, usually with **no terminal value**, by **DCF** or a **multiple** from comparable assets. Reduce value for **enforcement costs** and **infringement**.

**Brand name and similar:** **capital investment** (capitalise past spend, such as advertising; **least subjective** but far from market value), **DCF** (the **extra cash flow** attributable to the asset) or **relative** (compare firms **with and without** the brand).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A franchisee pays an initial charge and an annual fee in return for the brand, support and advertising.

items.title: Valuing real estate firms
items.core_explanation_md:
Real and financial assets share the principle that **value depends on cash flows, growth and risk**, so **intrinsic and relative valuation** apply.

**Differences:** **buildings have a finite life**, but **land lasts for ever** and can dominate the **terminal value**.

**Cost of equity:** use **CAPM or multifactor models**. Critics say property investors are **not diversified**; the courseware replies that concentration is a **choice**, property can be **subdivided and securitised**, and **diversified institutions** (REITs, partnerships) are likely to be the **marginal investors**. **Beta** for real assets is hard to measure for lack of a **price history** against an index.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The value of the land component may matter more than the building in the final value.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Because land has an endless life while buildings wear out.

items.title: Valuing a start-up: reinvestment and survival
items.core_explanation_md:
**Information is thin**, so use the **latest twelve months**, peer margins and bottom-up betas.

**Reinvestment when earnings are negative:** **expected reinvestment = expected change in revenue / (sales-to-capital ratio)**. A ratio of **5** means **Rs 2 lakh of capital for each Rs 10 lakh of extra revenue**.

**Growth** (when earnings are positive): **expected growth = reinvestment rate x return on capital**; in **stable growth**: **reinvestment rate = stable growth / stable ROC**.

**Survival:** **value of firm = P(survive) x DCF value + (1 - P(survive)) x distress or liquidation value.**

**Terminal value** holds most of the value, so the **growth and margin assumptions** matter most.

items.title: Financial service companies: dividend model inputs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Special features:** **debt is the raw material**, so debt and reinvestment are hard to define; **heavy regulation and capital adequacy norms**; **loan loss provisioning**; **difficulty choosing multiples**.

**Inputs for the dividend model:** **bottom-up beta** (average levered beta of comparables); **payout ratio including buybacks** (use a **composite over several years**); **growth = retention ratio x ROE**; with changing ROE: **retention x ROE(t+1) + (ROE(t+1) - ROE(t)) / ROE(t)**.

**Stable growth:** **payout ratio = 1 - g / ROE(stable)**, with beta moving towards 1.

items.title: Asset-based valuation of a financial institution
items.core_explanation_md:
Value the **loan portfolio** at **fair market value**: the **present value of its coupons at the market rate plus the present value of the principal**. Then **deduct deposits, debt and other claims** to get the **equity**.

A loan book earning **more than the market rate** is worth **more than book value**.

**Drawbacks:** it ignores **future growth and excess returns**, and it is **hard for firms in many businesses** (insurance, banking, investment banking) at once.

items.title: Equity as a call option in distressed firms
items.core_explanation_md:
For a **distressed** firm with large debt, equity holders have **limited liability** and the option to **liquidate**.

**Payoff to equity = V - D if V > D; 0 if V is at most D**, where **V** is the firm value and **D** the **face value of debt and other claims**. The **exercise price** is the **debt's face value**; the option **expires when the debt matures**.

**Implications:** equity can have value **even when V is below D** (time value), and **higher risk can raise equity value**, unlike in DCF.

items.title: Cash, cross holdings and consolidated versus separate valuation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Non-operating assets:** **cash and near-cash**, **stakes in other firms**, **idle land**, **surplus pension assets**.

**Why hold cash (Keynes):** **transactions**, **precaution**, **speculation**; also **managers may hoard**. Cash needs are **higher for cash businesses** (restaurants), **lower for firms with large transactions** and fall with **digital payments**.

**Consolidated valuation:** cash is treated as **inside** the firm: earnings include **interest on cash**; beta is a **weighted average** for the operating assets and the cash; so cash is **not added a second time**.

**Separate valuation:** **operating assets only**; **exclude interest on cash**; **add cash** to the value of operations.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Both routes should give the same value if applied consistently.

items.title: Warrants and convertibles
items.core_explanation_md:
A **convertible bond or preferred share** carries a **call option** to convert into equity at a **fixed price**.

Because its value **depends on the equity value**, it **cannot simply be deducted as debt** from enterprise value. If an **offer price exceeds the conversion price**, treating all convertibles as **converted** is reasonable.

items.title: Cyclical firms: normalising earnings
items.core_explanation_md:
Earnings in the **base year** can mislead for cyclical firms. **Remedies:** **adjust expected growth** (for example **higher near-term growth** when earnings are depressed), or **normalise earnings**: **what would the firm earn in a typical year?**

**Methods:** **average earnings over a full cycle** (**five to ten years**); **average the ROC or margin** over past periods and **apply it to current capital or revenue**, which adjusts for **current size** (revenue-based margins are **harder to manipulate**); and if recovery takes **several periods**, **reduce value for the delay**.

**Normalised earnings = average return on capital x current capital.**
